groups.label: Boyd / Bantry coverage
groups.definition: Reports, printed challenge and later related account concerning the expedition; not a single verified event.

groups.label: Boyd fleet report
groups.definition: Corresponding core fleet report; includes the edition with an appended challenge.

groups.label: Later fleet-return account
groups.definition: Later related account concerning the main body returning to Brest; no explicit retraction assigned.

groups.label: Tenerife defeat report
groups.definition: Printings of a Norfolk report, from a passenger on the Danish ship Christian Haven, that the British attack on Santa Cruz de Tenerife (July 1797) was driven off. Other Tenerife accounts in the collection are different texts and are not included.

groups.label: Duncan's Camperdown dispatches
groups.definition: Printings of Admiral Duncan's official dispatches on the defeat of the Dutch fleet off Camperdown (11 October 1797), from the London Gazette Extraordinary. Earlier first-news reports are not included.

groups.label: Algerine–Sicilian sea battle
groups.definition: Printings of a Civitavecchia report (30 June 1797) of a battle near Messina between an Algerine cruiser and a ship of the King of the Two Sicilies. The battle itself is not independently verified.

groups.label: Hermione mutiny
groups.definition: Reports of the mutiny on the British frigate Hermione (September 1797) and her delivery to the Spanish at La Guaira: first rumours, the detailed 'Particulars', and a follow-up.

groups.label: 'Particulars of the mutiny'
groups.definition: Printings of the detailed account of the Hermione mutiny first printed in Philadelphia on 16 November 1797.

groups.label: Barney escapes the blockade
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of Commodore Barney's letter of 21 August 1797 on escaping a seven-month blockade.

groups.label: Sonthonax leaves Saint-Domingue
groups.definition: Reports (September–October 1797) that the commissioner Sonthonax had sailed for France and Toussaint Louverture held the chief command.

groups.label: Quito earthquake
groups.definition: Printings of a Quito account (6 February 1797), via Jamaica, of the earthquake of 4 February.

groups.label: Peace / Cayenne context
groups.definition: Research collection of a seizure report and decree/commentary. Membership does not assert a legal or causal link.

groups.label: Peace seizure report
groups.definition: Corresponding reports about the named Peace account attributed to Whitney; excludes unresolved later same-name leads.

groups.label: Cayenne decree and commentary
groups.definition: Printed translated decree and attached allegation; original decree and itemized allegations remain unresolved.

groups.label: Peace and Plenty boarding
groups.definition: Printed accounts of the brig Peace and Plenty (Capt. Dunbar) being boarded and plundered by a French privateer, October 1797. A different vessel from the brig Peace (Capt. Allen). The accounts are not independently verified.

groups.label: Peace and Plenty report
groups.definition: Corresponding versions of the 'Piracy and Cruelty' marine report with Dunbar's quoted statement. Excludes the condensed 16 October retelling.

groups.label: Brothers boarded by privateer
groups.definition: Printings of Captain Kennard's report that the brig Brothers was boarded by a privateer on the way from Grenada to Portsmouth, N.H. (September 1797). Not independently verified.

groups.label: Two Sisters wreck
groups.definition: Printed accounts of the Rhode Island ship Two Sisters found wrecked off Bantry Bay in August 1797: a reprinted hand-bill and a summary attributed to the Irish papers. Different wording; the wreck itself is not independently verified.

groups.label: French captures at Havana
groups.definition: Printings of a Charleston report (September 1797) that more than a hundred American vessels had been carried into Havana by French privateers.

groups.label: Adams's farewell to the Senate
groups.definition: Printings of Vice President Adams's farewell address to the Senate (15 February 1797), plus the Senate's answer where printed separately.

groups.label: Special session of Congress, 1797
groups.definition: The special session of 1797: Adams's summoning proclamation (25 March), his speech (16 May) and the House's answer. Contains the speech, proclamation and answer groups.

groups.label: Adams's speech to Congress
groups.definition: Printings of President Adams's speech of 16 May 1797 opening the special session of Congress. Pages that only quote phrases from it are not included.

groups.label: Proclamation summoning Congress
groups.definition: Printings of Adams's proclamation of 25 March 1797 convening Congress on 15 May.

groups.label: House's answer to the special-session speech
groups.definition: Printings of the House of Representatives' answer to Adams's speech of 16 May 1797, in draft and final form.

groups.label: Blount affair
groups.definition: The Blount affair in the 1797 papers: the letter made public (July), Blount's welcome home at Knoxville (September), and the House committee's report (December). Contains those three groups; the wider coverage is not included.

groups.label: Blount letter made public
groups.definition: Printings of Senator William Blount's intercepted letter to the interpreter James Carey (July 1797): the letter as a document, and a Philadelphia report that introduces and quotes it. The wider Blount affair coverage is not included.

groups.label: Blount's welcome at Knoxville
groups.definition: Printings of a Knoxville report (18 September 1797) of Blount's welcome home.

groups.label: House committee report on Blount
groups.definition: Reports of the House committee's evidence report on Blount, 4 December 1797: a fuller account and a shorter summary.

groups.label: Andrew Brown house fire
groups.definition: Reports of the fire at the Philadelphia house of the printer Andrew Brown (27 January 1797) and notices of his death a week later. Several different texts.

groups.label: Opening of Congress, November 1797
groups.definition: Printings of Adams's speech opening the second session of the Fifth Congress (23 November 1797), the Senate's and House's answers, and his reply to the House.

groups.label: Kościuszko's land warrant
groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia item (September 1797): Kościuszko is offered a land warrant and back pay for his Revolutionary War service and declines the money.

groups.label: Jefferson's letter to Madison
groups.definition: Reports (January 1797) that Jefferson wrote to Madison about the election result, and a later report giving a different account of the letter.

groups.label: New Hampshire governor's address
groups.definition: Printings of the New Hampshire governor's address to the legislature, 22 November 1797.

observations.excerpt: Captain Boye positively asserts, that previous to his failing, accounts were received at the custom-house of Liverpool, of 17 sail of French vessels, men of war and transports, having a number of troops on board, destined for a descent on Ireland, being through gusts of weather blown into Bantry Bay, most of them distressed; some of the people went on shore, were made prisoners, and sent to Dublin; from the situation of the place the whole must inevitably be captured. They intended to have effected a landing at Londonderry in the North of Ireland.
observations.summary: Boyd's account of the French fleet at Bantry Bay.
observations.note: Scan: dismasted; RevX: distressed. The capture statement is a prediction.

observations.excerpt: Capt. Boyd, positively asserts, that previous to his sailing, accounts were received at the custom house of Liverpool, of 17 sail of French vessels, men of war and transports, having a number of troops on board, destined for a DESCENT ON IRELAND, being through stress of weather, blown into Bantry Bay, most of them dismasted; some of the people went on shore, were made prisoners, and went to Dublin; from the situation of the place the whole must inevitably be captured. They intended to have effected a landing at Londonderry in the North of Ireland. [NOTE. Capt. Boyd failed from Liverpool on the 29th December, and the French fleet left Brest, on the 26th of the same month: How then is it possible they should have reached Ireland in 3 days, and the accounts from thence received at Liverpool? Can it be thought that 20,000 French troops, and 17 ships of the line, have surrendered to the inhabitants of Bantry, whose population does not exceed 10,000 souls? It is more natural to think the French have taken that town.—Why were those 20,000 French sent to Dublin, 154 miles from Bantry Bay, and not to Cork, that lies but 9 miles from it? Can it be presumed, that the French fleet, in order to effect a landing at Londonderry, had entered the channel of Ireland so full of dangers, instead of sailing westward, on the main; a route much shorter and less difficult, free from the dangers of the channel, and which would not have exposed them to discovery from Liverpool or Dublin, and meet with every obstacle, that could have frustrated their design. CHRONICLE.]
observations.summary: The report appears with an appended challenge.
observations.note: Printed CHRONICLE challenge; objections are not independently adjudicated. Some failed forms read sailed in the scan.

observations.excerpt: Of the intelligence brought by the late arrivals, the most important relates to the French expedition against Ireland. By comparing the various accounts it appears, that the French failed from Brest with a view of invading Ireland. Their force consisted of about 50 sail, including transports, of which 17 were of the line and about 25,000 men on board. They failed in three divisions, under the command of De Galle, Bouvet and Neilly; the land troops under the orders of Gen. Hoche. They had scarcely left the port when bad weather dispersed them. Chief part of the fleet however, rendezvoused at Bantry Bay, but the frigate la Fraternite, on board of which were the commanders of the fleet and land forces not joining the fleet, after some delay they left the bay without molestation, except from the winds and by the best and latest accounts, reached Brest in divisions, without material loss. The Fraternite was one of the vessels to return. The expedition appears to have caused great alarm in Ireland and England. Had not the elements conspired against the French, little doubt can be entertained but they would have been successful. The expedition appears to have been planned on a large scale. The Toulon fleet which came round to L'Orient, and the armament at Dunkirk were probably to co-operate. The French appear still to have an expedition to Ireland in contemplation. A Paris date of January 29, mentions the arrival of Gen. Hoche in that capital, to give an account of his expedition.
observations.summary: Two weeks after printing Boyd's capture prediction, the Patowmac Guardian prints a summary saying the fleet dispersed and returned to Brest.
observations.note: The same summary the Kentucky Gazette printed on 19 April (H007), here 20 days earlier under a Martinsburg dateline. Neither paper names a source, so the copying route is unknown. The wording differs: Kentucky adds 'We have collected under this head…' and 'Notwithstanding the above failure'; this version adds the Fraternité's return, the 'great alarm' sentences and a Paris date about Hoche.

observations.excerpt: Of the intelligence brought by the late arrivals, the most important relates to the French expedition against Ireland. We have collected under this head, every interesting detail we have been able to meet with. By comparing the various accounts, it appears, that the French force when it failed from Brest, consisted of about 50 sail, including transports, of which 17 were of the line, and had on board 25,000 men.—They failed in three divisions, under the command of De Galles, Bouvet and Neuilly; the land troops under the command of general Hoche. They had scarcely left the port when bad weather dispersed them. Chief part of the fleet however rendezvoused at Bantry Bay, but the frigate la Fraternite, on board of which were the commanders of the fleet and land forces, not joining the fleet, after some delay left the Bay, without molestation, except by the wind, and by the best and latest accounts, reached Brest, in divisions without material loss. The expedition appears to have been planned on a large scale. The Toulon fleet which came round to l'Orient, and the armament at Dunkirk were probably to co-operate. Notwithstanding the above failure, the French appear still to have an expedition to Ireland in contemplation.
observations.summary: A later account describes the main body's return to Brest.
observations.note: Later account concerning the main body returning to Brest; no explicit retraction.

observations.excerpt: NORFOLK, September 28. By a gentleman passenger in the Danish ship, Christians Haven, Capt. observations.excerpt: Thursday evening arrived the brig Maria, capt. Whitney, in 34 days from Cayenne. By him we are advised of the seizure and prompt condemnation of the brig Peace, capt. Samuel Allen, of this port; vessel, cargo, and specie on board, valued at 25,000 dollars. Capt. Allen was from Dover, bound for Surinam, but touched at Cayenne, where he had been several days before the seizure was made. The pretext was, his being from an English port.
observations.summary: A report of the seizure of Peace, attributed to Captain Whitney.
observations.note: Publication date differs from the internal Providence dateline of May 13. The seizure date is not supplied.

observations.excerpt: Thursday evening arrived the brig Maria, Capt. Whitney, in 34 days from Cayenne. By him we are advised of the seizure and prompt condemnation of the brig Peace, Capt. Samuel Allen, of this Port; vessel, cargo and specie on board, valued at 25000 dollars. Capt. Allen was from Dover, bound for Surinam, but touched at Cayenne, where he had been several days before the seizure was made. The pretext was, his being from an English port. [We are respectably informed that as some specie which had been on board of the above vessel, was missing at the time of capture, the Capt. having purchased certain articles and remitted them to his owner, they obliged him to draw a bill on his Employer for the amount so remitted. [Mercury.]

observations.note: The shared report and appended commentary are distinct textual elements. The commentary is not independently corroborated.

observations.excerpt: It is easy to perceive, that the American papers, cited in this decree, are the Jacobin Gazettes of the United States, and that the instances quoted, are seven out of eight, false and scandalous. It is also very evident, that the French Agents, in the United States, have published those very accounts in the Aurora , Argus , Chronicle , and other hiring papers, merely to give a pretext to the plunderers in the West-Indies, to seize and confiscate American vessels, and that the Printers of them have been base and sordid enough to send them those papers, in order that they may be adduced as documents, to justify their infamy! The American merchants and seamen, who suffer under the piracies in the West-Indies, now look to those Printers as the Authors of their misery; and were they to prosecute for reparation, an honest jury would do no less than grant a verdict in their favor.
observations.summary: A translated Cayenne decree with an attached editorial allegation.
observations.note: A contextual document, not an established legal cause of the Peace seizure. The original decree and itemized allegations remain unresolved.

observations.excerpt: PIRACY AND CRUELTY. Same day, brig Peace and Plenty, Dunbar, St. Croix, 24 days. In lat. 23, N. long. 65, 35, W. was boarded by a French privateer brig, from Guadalupe, under English colours. The particulars of the treatment which capt. D. received, is thus recorded by him.
observations.summary: Captain Dunbar of the brig Peace and Plenty reports being boarded and plundered by a French privateer from Guadeloupe.
observations.note: The scan prints Dunbar's full quoted statement (about 350 words) after this introduction. The RevX transcription drops it; the CA transcription keeps it. The excerpt is limited to the RevX text, so read the statement on the scan.

observations.excerpt: BOSTON, OCT. 11. Fraternity.—Capt. Dunbar, from St. Croix, in lat. 23, N. long. 65, 35, W. was boarded by a French privateer brig, from Guadalupe, the capt. of which, with five of his crew, came on board and demanded Capt. D's papers; after examination, ordered his chests and trunks to be opened— took from them all the money and letters— took all the flock cabin stores, spare rigging, sails and blocks—one cask of rum, &c. —suffered his people to steal even knives and forks, spoons, tumblers, and every article remaining in the cabin. The privateer captain put on board us two seamen taken from the brig Favourite, Scituate, of Baltimore, and Mr. Taylor, supercargo, with a cargo of 50,000 dollars. He also wished to get rid of Capt. Scituate and Mr. Taylor, but they insisted on staying aboard the privateer and know the state of their property, which spirited behaviour produced a conduct unworthy a man, for on their refusal to quit the privateer, the capt. indignantly flogged them! Several other American masters and seamen were on board this privateer, among them was Mr. John Barnes, of Marblehead. Before the privateer left us, she took a loop from Rhode-Island, capt. Briggs, bound to Cape-Francois. The captain of the privateer to finish his brutal behaviour, threatened to punish capt. Dunbar—dismissed him with a curse on his country, and a determination to rob every American vessel that could not be made a prize of.
observations.summary: Three days later the same paper prints a shorter retelling of Dunbar's account under a Boston, Oct. 11 dateline, headed 'Fraternity'.
observations.note: A condensed paraphrase rather than the quoted statement, so it belongs to the boarding group but not the core report group.

observations.excerpt: Same day, brig Peace and Plenty, Dunbar, St. Croix, 24 days. In lat. 23, N. long. 65, 55, W. was boarded by a French privateer brig, from Guadalupe, under English colors. The particulars of the treatment which Capt. D. received, is thus recorded by him. "The capt. of this privateer came on board, with five of his crew, and demanded my papers; after examination, ordered all my trunks and chests to be opened, and took from them all the money they contained, with the letters, which he opened; he took all our stock, and cabin stores, with all the spare running rigging, sails and blocks, and cut one studling-fall from the yard; he also took one cask of rum, belonging to the cargo, and a case that belonged to capt. Haynes, who was to have come passenger, contents unknown. After plundering us of the above articles, he suffered his people to rob us of what they pleased, and so fully devoted were they to the business of thieving, that they took every article they could find, even to the knives, forks, spoons and tumblers, and in fact every article remaining in the cabin.—He then put two seamen on board, that were taken a few days before from the brig Favorite, Sisson, of Baltimore, master, and Mr. Taylor, supercargo, with a cargo of 50,000 dollars. The capt. of the privateer, wished to put capt. Sisson, and Mr. Taylor on board my vessel, but they insisted on staying aboard the privateer, and demanded to know the fate of their property, which spirited behaviour produced on the commander of the privateer, a conduct unworthy a man, for on their refusal to quit the privateer he inhumanly flogged them! Besides capt. Sisson, there were several other American masters and seamen on board the privateer, names, except one, not to be ascertained, this individual's name was John Barnes, of Marblehead:—A few hours previous to our being boarded, the privateer took a sloop from Rhode-Island, capt. Briggs, bound to Cape Francois, who, he said, was a good prize. To add insult to our misfortune this inhuman pirate threatened to take me on board his vessel, and inflict an ignominious punishment on me; and finished his brutal behaviour by dismissing me, with a curse on my country, and a declared determination to rob every American vessel he could not make a prize of.
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette prints the full report with Dunbar's quoted statement.
observations.note: Corresponds closely to the Gazette of the United States text of 13 October as printed on the scan.

observations.excerpt: Piracy and Cruelty. Arrived, brig Peace and Plenty, Dunbar, St. Caoix, 24 day. In lat. 23 N. long. 65. 35. W. was boarded by a French privateer brig, from Guadaloupe under English colours. The particulars of the treatment which Capt. D. received, are thus recorded by him. "The capt. of this privateer came on board, with five of his crew, and demanded my papers; after examination, ordered all my trunks and chests to be opened, and took from them all the money they contained, with the letters, which he opened; he took all our stock, and cabin stores, with all the spare running rigging, sails and blocks, and cut one fludding sail from the yard; he also took one cask of rum, belonging to the cargo, and a cask that belonged to Capt. Hayoc, who was to have come passenger, contents unknown. After plundering us of the above articles, he suffered his people to rob us of what they pleased; and fully devoted were they to the business of thieving, that they took every article they could find, even to the knives, forks, spoons, and tumblers, and in fact every article remaining in the cabin. He then put two seamen on board, who were taken a few days before from the brig Favorite, Siffon of Baltimore, master, and Mr. Taylor, supercargo, with a cargo of 30,000 dollars. The Capt. of the privateer wished to put Capt. Siffon, and Mr. Taylor on board my vessel; but they insisted on staying aboard the privateer, and demanded to know the fate of their property, which spirited behaviour produced on the commander of the privateer, a conduct unbecoming a man; for on their refusal to quit the privateer, he inhumanly fluted them! Besides Capt. Siffon, there were several other American masters and seamen on board the privateer, names, except one, not to be ascertained, this individual's name was John Barns, of Marsthead. A few hours previous to our being boarded, the privateer took a sloop from Rhode-Island, Captain Briggs, bound to Cape Francois, who, he said, was a good prize. To add insult to our misfortune, this inhuman pirate threatened to take me on board his vessel, and inflict an ignominious punishment on me; and finished his brutal behavior by dismissing me, with a curse on my country, and a declared determination to rob every American vessel he could not make a prize of."
observations.summary: The Eagle prints the full report under a Boston, Oct. 8 dateline.
observations.note: 'St. Caoix' and '24 day' are printed that way in the paper. The Eagle prints a Boston execution report directly after it; that story also appears in the New Hampshire Gazette of 17 October.

observations.excerpt: Dreadful SHIPWRECK!! The following account of the shipwreck of the Two Sisters of Rhode-Island, is taken from a Hand-Bill published at BANTRY-BAY, AUG. 12, '97. This morning about 2 o'clock, as some of our fishing boats were working out between the heads, they saw a large ship in the Offing, seemingly in great distress. They stood for the ship, and about 10 o'clock, they boarded her; but there was only one living man on board. She proves to be the Two Sisters, from Rhode-Island, bound for Bristol, and had been out five weeks:—Such a wreck, surely never was seen before! her mizen-mast was all split to pieces, and her main-mast was a stern hanging by some of the wreck; her foremast was also split to pieces, and her fore-top-mast gone by the cap in her steerage or half deck. There were seven men burnt to a coal, and the mate lying under the windlass dead; and as for the Captain, we have no account of him, only the young man found with the wreck says that the Captain and all hands were on deck when some dreadful thunder and lightning came on; and that there were six men on the main-top-sail yard when the mainmast went over the side, and that they were all lost. He says the Captain was on the quarter deck when the mast went, but as he did not see him afterwards, he thinks the wreck hauled him overboard.
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette reprints a Bantry Bay hand-bill dated 12 August 1797 on the wreck of the Rhode Island ship Two Sisters.
observations.note: Hand-bill account: lightning struck the ship, one man survived, seven men were burnt and the mate died. The captain is missing.

observations.excerpt: A melancholy narrative appears in the lists of the disasters of the American ship Two Sisters, of Rhode-Island, bound for Bristol, off Bantry Bay, in August last. On appearance of distress, she was boarded by some people from the land—they found her mizen mast shivered to pieces, her main mast overboard, hanging astern, and her fore topsail gone by the cap—only one living man was found in the wreck, who informed that the ship had been struck by lightning, and that there were six men on the main topsail yard when the mainmast went over the side, all of whom were lost, together with the master of the vessel, who was wanted overboard—seven men were burnt to a coal, and the mate dead; the ship had four feet water in her hold when boarded—was from the Bay of Honduras, with oil, whale bone, logwood and mahogany; the captain's name Gilbert; owner Mr. Mosely of Rhode Island—the people of the coast hauled the vessel up on the beach; the bottom appeared to be in tolerable condition; but masts, spars, sails, &c. worth nothing.
observations.summary: The Gazette of the United States summarizes the same wreck, citing the Irish papers, and adds the cargo, captain and owner.
observations.note: Different wording from the hand-bill, but the details correspond: six men on the main topsail yard, seven men burnt and the mate dead.

observations.excerpt: TUESDAY, May 16. The Senate attended in the Representatives Chamber, and at 12 o'clock, the PRESIDENT delivered the following SPEECH. observations.excerpt: January 27. MELANCHOLLY AND DISTRESSING. This morning about a quarter before 6 o'clock, Fire broke out in the lower part of the Dwelling-House of Mr. Andrew Brown, Printer, of this city. The usual spirited exertions of the Citizens prevented the flames from extending to the adjoining houses—and Mr. Brown's Printing Office escaped uninjured. Every humane bosom must be wrung with anguish at the recital of the shocking catastrophe consequent to this event. Mr. Brown, his apprentices, and some other domestics of the family escaped with their lives, by rushing thro' the flames or jumping from the windows—Mr. Brown is very much bruised and is dangerously ill
observations.summary: First report of the fire at the Philadelphia house of the printer Andrew Brown on 27 January 1797.
observations.note: Found by phrase search, not by the reuse family. The report goes on to describe what happened to Mrs Brown and her three children.

observations.excerpt: The mournful tale of the dreadful catastrophe which lately overwhelmed the family of Mr. Brown, the printer of the Philadelphia Gazette, was heightened by the death of Mr. Brown himself, who expired on Saturday morning.
observations.summary: The Gazette of the United States reports Andrew Brown's own death after the fire.
observations.note: A shorter, differently worded notice than the version the other papers carry.

observations.excerpt: PHILADELPHIA, Jan. 28. Melancholy Event. Never since we have assumed the office of recording passing events to the public, have we entered on the task with more painful sensations, than on the melancholy occasion we have now to mention. About 5 o'clock yesterday morning the house of Mr. ANDREW BROWN, Printer of the Philadelphia Gazette, in this city, was discovered to be on fire. How it originated or progressed, we have not correct information, but the melancholy and almost unparalleled catastrophe, is, we fear, too certain. Mrs. BROWN, two daughters, one son, and a negro boy, have perished in the flames. Two apprentices have suffered severely, and Mr. BROWN is so dreadfully burnt, that but faint hopes of his recovery are entertained.
observations.summary: A different Philadelphia report of the fire: it says Mrs Brown, two daughters, a son and a Black boy died in the flames.
observations.note: Found by phrase search. Different wording from the Patowmac Guardian report.

observations.excerpt: The mournful catastrophe which has lately overwhelmed the family of Mr. Brown, the printer of the Philadelphia Gazette, in this city, attained its full height on Saturday morning, by the death of Mr. Brown himself of an inflammation of the lungs, occasioned by the large quantity of smoke and mephitic air which he had inhaled, before he was extricated from the fire.
observations.summary: The Virginia Argus prints the longer notice of Brown's death.
observations.note: Same wording as the Patowmac Guardian and New Hampshire Gazette notices.

observations.excerpt: PHILADELPHIA, February 6. The mournful catastrophe which has lately overwhelmed the family of Mr. Brown, the printer of the Philadelphia Gazette, in this city, attained its full height on Saturday morning, by the death of Mr. Brown himself, of an inflammation of the lungs, occasioned by the large quantities of smoke and mephitic air which he had imbibed, before he was extricated from the fire.
observations.summary: The Patowmac Guardian prints the notice of Brown's death.
observations.note: Same notice; Philadelphia, February 6 dateline.

observations.excerpt: The mournful catastrophe which has lately overwhelmed the family of Mr. Brown, the printer of the Philadelphia Gazette, in this city, attained its full height on Saturday morning, by the death of Mr. Brown himself, of an inflammation of the lungs, occasioned by the large quantity of fumes and mephitic air which he had imbibed, before he was extricated from the fire.
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette prints the notice of Brown's death, four weeks after the fire.
observations.note: Same notice as the Virginia Argus and Patowmac Guardian versions.

observations.excerpt: PRESIDENT'S SPEECH. THIS DAY, At Twelve o'Clock, the PRESIDENT of the United States, met both Houses of Congress, in the Chamber of the Representatives, where he addressed them in the following SPEECH. Gentlemen of the Senate, and Gentlemen of the House of Representatives, I was for some time apprehensive, that it would be necessary, on account of the contagious sickness, which afflicted the city of Philadelphia, to convene the National Legislature at some other place;
observations.summary: Adams's speech opening the second session of Congress, which met in Philadelphia after the yellow fever.
observations.note: Earliest printing in the collection, on the day of the speech.

observations.excerpt: The Senate, in a body, this day waited on the President of the United States, with the following answer to his address to both Houses, at the opening of the present session. To the PRESIDENT of the United States. SIR, THE communications you have thought proper to make in your speech to both houses of Congress, on the opening of their session, afford additional proofs of the attention, integrity and firmness which have always marked your official character.
observations.summary: The Senate's answer to the speech.
observations.note: Printed the day it was presented.

observations.excerpt: Mr. OTIS, from the committee appointed to draft an address in answer to the speech of the President of the United States, reported the following, which was twice read, and referred to a committee of the whole for to-morrow: SIR, WHILE our sympathy is excited by the recent sufferings of the citizens of Philadelphia, we participate in the satisfaction which you are pleased to express, that the duration of the late calamity was so limited
observations.summary: The House committee's draft answer, opening with sympathy for Philadelphia's sufferings.
observations.note: The draft as first reported; the House amended it before passing.

observations.excerpt: To which the President made the following reply: Gentlemen of the House of Representatives, I RECEIVE this address from the House of Representatives of the United States with peculiar pleasure.
observations.summary: Adams's reply to the House's answer.
observations.note: Printed the day after it was given.

observations.excerpt: On Thursday at 12 o'clock, the Senate having assembled in the Representatives' Hall, The President came in, accompanied by his Secretary and the Heads of Departments, and delivered the following SPEECH. Gentlemen of the Senate, and Gentlemen of the House of Representatives, I WAS for some time apprehensive, that it would be necessary, on account of the contagious sickness which afflicted the city of Philadelphia, to convene the national Legislature, at some other place.
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette prints the speech.
observations.note: Same speech; only the opening is excerpted.

observations.excerpt: At 12 o'clock, the Senate having assembled in the Representatives' Hall, the President came in, accompanied by his Secretary and the heads of departments, and delivered the following SPEECH: Gentlemen of the Senate, and Gentlemen of the House of Representatives, I WAS for some time apprehensive, that it would be necessary, on account of the contagious sickness which afflicted the city of Philadelphia, to convene the National Legislature, at some other place.
observations.summary: The Mirror prints the speech.
observations.note: The speech continues on page 3.

observations.excerpt: The following is the address of the Senate, in answer to the Speech delivered by the President of the United States, at the opening of the Session: TO THE PRESIDENT of the United States. SIR, THE communications you have thought proper to make in your Speech to both Houses of Congress on the opening of their present session, afford additional proofs of the attention, integrity, and firmness, which have always marked your official character.
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette prints the Senate's answer.
observations.note: Same page as the House's answer.

observations.excerpt: The Answer of the House stands as follows:— SIR, WHILE our sympathy is excited by the recent sufferings of the citizens of Philadelphia, we participate in the satisfaction which you are pleased to express, that the duration of the late calamity was so limited
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette prints the House's answer as passed.
observations.note: After a report of the amendment debate.

observations.excerpt: The following is the Address of the Senate in answer to the Speech delivered by the President of the United States, at the opening of the session:— To the PRESIDENT of the U. STATES. SIR, THE communications you have thought proper to make in your speech, to both Houses of Congress, on the opening of their present session, afford additional proofs of the attention, integrity and firmness, which have always marked your official character.
observations.summary: The Mirror prints the Senate's answer.
observations.note: Same page as the House's answer.

observations.excerpt: Then answer was then reported to the House, and passed in the following words:— SIR, WHILE our sympathy is excited by the recent sufferings of the citizens of Philadelphia, we participate in the satisfaction which you are pleased to express; that the duration of the late calamity was so limited
observations.summary: The Mirror prints the House's answer as passed.
observations.note: After a report of the amendment debate.

observations.excerpt: The President's Reply, to the Answer of the House. Gentlemen of the House of Representatives, I RECEIVE this Address from the House of Representatives of the United States with peculiar pleasure.
observations.summary: The Mirror prints Adams's reply to the House.
observations.note: Follows Adams's reply to the Senate on the same page.

observations.excerpt: To which the President returned the following answer, Gentlemen of the House of Representatives. I received this address from the House of Representatives of the United States with peculiar pleasure.
observations.summary: The Eagle prints Adams's reply to the House.
observations.note: Same reply.

observations.excerpt: General Kosciusko, we hear, has left the city, on a visit to General White, of New Brunswick. Before he left town, we understand, a gentleman in office presented him with a land warrant, to which he was entitled by his services, and intimated there was a sum of money due to him, for his services in the cause of this country.
observations.summary: General Kościuszko, visiting Philadelphia, is offered a land warrant and back pay for his Revolutionary War service.
observations.note: Printed beside a yellow-fever burial report signed by Stephen Girard.

observations.excerpt: PHILADELPHIA, Sept. 6. General Kosciuszko, we hear, has left the city, on a visit to Gen. White, of New Brunswick. Before he left town, we understand, a gentleman in office presented him with a land warrant, to which he was entitled by his services, and intimated there was a sum of money due to him, for his services in the cause of this country.
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette prints the same item.
observations.note: Same item.

observations.excerpt: General Kosciuszko, we hear, has left the city on a visit to his friend General Gates, in the state of New York. Before he left town, we understand, a gentleman in office presented him with a land warrant, to which he was entitled by his services, and intimated there was a sum of money due to him, for his services in the cause of this country.
observations.summary: The Kentucky Gazette prints the item.
observations.note: Says he left to visit 'his friend General Gates, in the state of New York', not General White of New Brunswick.

observations.excerpt: We are informed, and from an authority which we rely on, that Mr. Jefferson has written to Mr. Madison on the subject of the late election; and given it as his opinion, that Mr. Adams was the only person who ought to have been elected President; and further, that he is the only person under whom he would accept the Vice-Presidency. If our information is accurate, the acceptance of Mr. J. will be unquestionable.
observations.summary: Report that Jefferson wrote to Madison that Adams alone ought to have been elected, and that he would serve as Vice President under him.
observations.note: No dateline in this printing.

observations.excerpt: BOSTON, January 14. We are informed, and from an authority which we rely on, that Mr. Jefferson has written to Mr. Madison on the subject of the late election; and given it as his opinion, that Mr. Adams was the only person who ought to have been elected President; and further, that he is the only person under whom he would accept the Vice-Presidency. If our information is accurate, the acceptance of Mr. J. will be unquestionable.
observations.summary: The Gazette of the United States prints the report under a Boston dateline.
observations.note: Same report.

observations.excerpt: STOCKBRIDGE, January 23. It is true that Mr. Jefferson has written to Mr. Madison, requesting him, (for reasons which he details,) if there should be an equal vote between Mr. Adams and himself,
observations.summary: A Stockbridge report confirms the letter and gives a different account of what it asked.
observations.note: Different text: says the letter asked Madison to act if the vote was tied.

observations.excerpt: WASHINGTON CITY, January 28. We are informed, and from an authority which we rely on, that Mr. Jefferson has written to Mr. Madison on the subject of the late election; and given it as his opinion, that Mr. Adams was the only person who ought to have been elected President; and further, that he is the only person under whom he would accept the Vice-Presidency. If our information is accurate, the acceptance of Mr. Jefferson will be unquestion
observations.summary: The Patowmac Guardian prints the report under a Washington City dateline.
observations.note: Same report; spells out 'Mr. Jefferson' where others have 'Mr. J.'.

observations.excerpt: The honorable Senate being assembled with the House in the Representatives chamber, His Excellency the Governor came in, escorted by the committee, and delivered to both branches of the Legislature the following ADDRESS: Fellow citizens of the Senate, and of the House of Representatives. IN meeting you at this time when the tranquility, general health and prosperity of the State afford so much cause for mutual congratulation,
observations.summary: The New Hampshire governor's address opening the legislature's session, 22 November 1797.
observations.note: Printed in the legislature's journal.

observations.excerpt: The Senate being assembled with the House in the Representatives' Chamber, His Excellency the Governor came in, escorted by the committee, and delivered to both branches of the Legislature the following ADDRESS. Fellow Citizens of the Senate, and of the House of Representatives, IN meeting you at this time, when tranquility, general health and prosperity of the State afford so much cause for mutual congratulation,
observations.summary: The Mirror prints the governor's address.
observations.note: Same address.

observations.excerpt: PORTSMOUTH, (N.H.) Nov. 25. On Wednesday last agreeably to adjournment, the Hon. General Court convened in this town. The Hon. Senate being assembled with the house in the representatives chamber, His Excellency the Governor came in escorted by the committee, and addressed the Legislature with the following SPEECH: Fellow-Citizens of the Senate, and of the House of Representatives, In meeting you at this time when the tranquility, general health and prosperity of the state afford so much cause for mutual congratulation,
observations.summary: The Gazette of the United States in Philadelphia prints the New Hampshire governor's address.
observations.note: The only printing outside New Hampshire.
